identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Bhadrachalam is one of the principal Rama temples in India, popularly called Dakshina Ayodhya ('the Ayodhya of the South'). Its presiding image is the four-armed Vaikuntha Rama, seated with Sita on his lap and flanked by Lakshmana, an iconographic form distinct from the more common standing or two-armed Rama found elsewhere. The temple is closely linked to the 17th-century poet-devotee Bhadrachala Ramadasu (Kancharla Gopanna), whose Telugu devotional songs to Rama remain part of its musical tradition.

governance.founderPatron: Kancharla Gopanna (Bhadrachala Ramadasu), a 17th-century Golconda-era revenue official (tahsildar) who is documented to have spent large sums — including revenue funds he was not authorised to use — renovating and enlarging the temple, for which he was imprisoned roughly 12-14 years. Devotional accounts of a miraculous repayment of the debt, with Rama and Lakshmana appearing in the Sultan's dream, are traditional legend rather than documented history.

narrative.summaryIntro:
The Sri Sita Ramachandraswamy Temple at Bhadrachalam, on the banks of the Godavari river in Bhadradri Kothagudem district, Telangana, is one of the principal Rama temples in India and is popularly known as Dakshina Ayodhya. Its presiding deity is the four-armed Vaikuntha Rama, seated with Sita on his lap and flanked by Lakshmana — an iconographic form distinct from the standing or two-armed Rama images found at most other Rama temples.

The temple is closely associated with the 17th-century poet-devotee Kancharla Gopanna, known as Bhadrachala Ramadasu, who is credited with renovating and enlarging the shrine while serving as a Golconda-era revenue official. His Telugu devotional kirtanas to Rama remain part of the temple's musical tradition and are said to have influenced the Carnatic composer Tyagaraja. The temple is administered today by the Telangana State Endowments Department.
narrative.documentedHistory:
According to the itihasa (traditional narrative) recounted by the temple, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana passed through the Dandaka forest near the Godavari during their fourteen-year exile. A stone is said to have become the sage Bhadra through Rama's grace, and Bhadra's long penance on the Godavari bank is remembered as the origin of the hill on which the temple stands; the icon's later rediscovery is separately attributed in local tradition to a tribal woman, Pokala Dhammakka, who is said to have found it in an anthill. These are devotional accounts rather than datable events.

The documented history of the present temple begins in the 17th century. Kancharla Gopanna (c. 1620-1688), a Niyogi Brahmin later known as Bhadrachala Ramadasu, took up a revenue post at Bhadrachalam around 1650 through relatives who were ministers at the Qutb Shahi court, and was later tahsildar of the Palvoncha paragana. He spent substantial sums, including government revenue he was not authorised to use, renovating and enlarging the Sita Ramachandraswamy temple, and invited priestly families from the Ranganathaswamy temple at Srirangam to establish Pancharatra Agama worship there. For this unauthorised spending he was imprisoned at Golconda for roughly twelve to fourteen years under Sultan Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Tana Shah), the last ruler of the Qutb Shahi dynasty, and died in 1688. Multiple devotional accounts describe his release — including a story that Rama and Lakshmana appeared in the Sultan's dream and repaid the debt in gold coins, and alternative versions in which the Sultan freed him after an inquiry or out of clemency — but English-language secondary sources note plainly that these release narratives 'lack historical evidence,' and this record does not present any one version as settled fact. A widely repeated story that the poet-saint Kabir intervened on Gopanna's behalf is likewise treated by these sources as legend rather than history, and is chronologically difficult to reconcile with Kabir's own dates.

In the following centuries the temple continued to draw endowments and remained a site of institutional continuity: it stayed with the Hyderabad State in an 1860s boundary settlement even as surrounding territory passed to British administration, and its lands were merged into Khammam district in 1959. Government oversight of maintenance passed to the Andhra Pradesh Endowments ministry in 1958, and recorded repairs were carried out from 1960 under the endowments minister of the time. The temple withstood severe Godavari flash floods in August 1986, when the kalyana mandapam was inundated except for its gopuram but daily rituals continued. During the 2014 division of Andhra Pradesh, Bhadrachalam's location on the border between the two successor states made it a point of political contention, and it was ultimately retained within Telangana; the district of Bhadradri Kothagudem, containing Bhadrachalam, was created in the state's 2016 district reorganisation. The temple is administered today by the Telangana State Endowments Department.

openingHours.notes: Darshan is suspended for a midday closure from 1:00 PM to 3:00 PM; the temple reopens at 3:00 PM and closes for the night at 9:00 PM.
The official Arjitha Sevas schedule gives Sunday's Suprabhata Seva, and with it the temple's opening, as half an hour earlier than the rest of the week (4:00 AM instead of 4:30 AM).
Darshan is not offered during this window.

shrines.locationDescription: The first of the temple's three architectural divisions, believed by tradition to correspond to Bhadra's head; contains a rock said to bear Rama's footprints.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Vaikuntha Rama, with Sita and Lakshmana
shrines.locationDescription: The garbhagriha housing the four-armed Vaikuntha Rama with Sita on his lap and Lakshmana at his side; by tradition sited at the heart of Bhadra.
The main tower of the temple, at the third of its three architectural divisions, by tradition sited at Bhadra's feet.
A large entrance built in 1974 to manage pilgrim flow; devotees pass through it during Vaikuntha Ekadashi observances.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Hall for the Sita-Rama wedding festival
shrines.locationDescription: The hall used for the annual Sri Sitarama Kalyanotsavam; inundated except for its gopuram in the August 1986 Godavari floods.
Sub-shrine within the temple complex, listed among the devasthanam's constituent temples on the official portal.
Shrine on the Ranganayakula Gutta hillock, a higher point of the complex facing south.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Site associated with Rama's forest exile
shrines.locationDescription: A related shrine site, administered together with the main devasthanam, associated by tradition with the exile sojourn of Rama, Sita and Lakshmana.
Sub-shrine within the temple complex, listed among the devasthanam's constituent temples on the official portal.

poojas.description: The waking ritual that opens the day's worship. The official Arjitha Sevas schedule gives 4:30 AM Monday to Saturday and 4:00 AM on Sunday.
Morning food offering and associated rites.
Abhishekam performed at Bhadra's shrine, at the rock said to bear Rama's footprints.
Booked archana offered through most of the day in the antarala (the vestibule between sanctum and hall).
Recitation of the deity's thousand names.

The daily re-enactment of the wedding of Sita and Rama. The temple's own timings page gives 9:30-11:30 AM, while its Arjitha Sevas page gives the start as 9:00 AM; the discrepancy has not been resolved.
Evening seva involving the silver processional chariot/vehicle of the deity.
Circumambulation of the processional deity around the temple.
Processional worship of the deity on a vahana (vehicle).
Evening court-audience ritual for the deity.

poojas.description: The closing ritual of the day; the temple's timings page lists a nivedana bhogam from 8:30-9:00 PM after which the temple closes, while the Arjitha Sevas page lists Pavalimpu Seva at 9:00 PM.
Worship offered to cows, drawing on the tradition of cattle husbandry associated with the temple.
Archana with 108 names offered using a golden tulasi.
Archana with 108 names offered using golden flowers.

poojas.recurrence: Monthly, on the Pushyami Nakshatram day
poojas.description: Coronation ritual for the deity, performed on the monthly nakshatram day associated with Rama's own coronation.

poojas.recurrence: Monthly, on the Chitha Nakshatram day
poojas.description: Fire ritual dedicated to Vishnu's Sudarshana Chakra.

poojas.recurrence: Monthly, on the Bahula Ekadasi day
poojas.description: Archana offered with a lakh (100,000) applications of kumkum.

festivals.significance: The temple's principal annual festival, centred on the ceremonial wedding (Kalyanotsavam) of Sita and Rama, with associated rites including Ankurarpanam, Dwajarohanam, Mahapattabhishekam and Teppotsavam (float festival).

Includes a float festival (Teppotsavam) on the Godavari using the swan-shaped Hamsavahanam, and Rathotsavam (chariot festival) coinciding with Makar Sankranti. Per the Brahma Purana as cited by the temple's own account, devotees who worship Vaikuntha Rama on this day are held to attain salvation.
A spring festival including the Dolotsavam swing ritual for the deity and preparation of turmeric-based rites.
Marked by daily Ramayana recitation, weapon worship, and a night-time Ramlila; the deity is taken in procession on elephant and horse vehicles.

The article itself states that the stories of Gopanna's miraculous release 'lack historical evidence,' and this record follows that caution.

sources.claimScope: Biography of Kancharla Gopanna (Bhadrachala Ramadasu): birth c. 1620 in Nelakondapalli, his revenue-official career, his temple renovation and unauthorised use of government funds, imprisonment at Golconda, death in 1688, and the disputed authenticity of poems attributed to him.
sources.reliabilityNote: The article states his biography has been 'largely reconstructed from poems he composed,' indicating significant uncertainty in specific dates and events.
